posts.content:
I had Opus build a game that takes JIRA tickets from any of your real projects & converts them into dramatic audiologs that are the plot of a 2000s-era horror game set on a mysteriously abandoned space station.

Play a demo: wontfix-game.netlify.app

Github: github.com/emollick/aud...

I was interviewed in Vox about my new book, and a question on the meaning of work let me discuss something I have been thinking a lot about, comparing the logic of industrialization to the logic of craft: "You’re a hand-weaver in a world of power looms." www.vox.com/technology/5...

For Halloween, I asked Opus 5.5 to suggest a spooky project based on my existing work, and it came up with the idea of the ghost census. Pick a location to see how many people died within a 100 meters of it through all of history up to a century ago & get some example lives. ghost-census.netlify.app

The Pro series of GPT models continues to be really impressive for one-shot problems that involve complex calculations, references, or sophisticated ideas.

It isn't particularly fast (or particularly pleasant) to use but GPT-6 Astra Pro gives that "ask one question of the great oracle" feel.

If this holds up, it is big: "We asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to improve math. It directly changed only 0.016% of weights, fixing 0.8B's reasoning loops & improving math up to 6x and even instruction following 3x, without gradients or training." rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-...

I had Opus 5.5 create a site where you can see the fastest routes into every city in the US, figure out where in America is fairest to meet up, see the "watersheds" of the largest cities, and more: all-roads-lead-to.netlify.app  

(Inspired by the defunct Arterial Mapping site)

When you think about the Labs' weird approach to software releases (sudden changes, bad communication), it is worth remembering that a core belief is that these products are a temporary thing they have to do to raise money for a couple years until "true" AGI makes all products obsolete.

"Opus, great, now turn that into a movie, i know you can make it amazing. figure it out."

Yes, that was the only prompt
Opus 5.5: "Give me 10 brilliant ideas for a science fiction short short story, pick the most brilliant and execute it terribly"

Here is a mass attempted replication of old findings of LLMs with new models. Much conventional wisdom is outdated.

Recent models no longer invent citations and both hallucination rates & stereotyping has dropped. But they are still sycophantic & lean left.  zou-group.github.io/llm-claims-s...

We are in an era of flux & fighting over how AI should be used to review academic work & by whom.

But it is worth proving to yourself that yes, AI used properly can be very insightful at this, by asking GPT-6 Pro/Opus 5.5 High to give helpful, substantive feedback on one of your papers.

AI semiotics: cool paper suggests that AIs are strongly impacted by visual symbols in ways they do not always recognize in their own chains-of-thought. The way they react to those symbols is very different than how a human might interpret them as well. arxiv.org/pdf/2610.364...
Whatever role AI played as an issue in this election, I suspect it will play a larger role in every election to come, at least for the foreseeable future.

One ongoing frustration is the lack of effort I see being put towards near-term, achievable crash projects to do good with AI at a national scale, whether those efforts are by the AI labs or by policymakers & NGOs using free models.

We should be more ambitious about trying to solve hard problems.

As I have written many times in the past years, any potential financial downturn in AI stocks will not greatly change the AI trajectory

AI is not going away, companies are not slowing down adoption, nor is development slowing. We still need policy & effort so that AI is used to help us all thrive.

As a longtime reader (and writer of two small pieces in the 1990s) of WIRED, I was curious if the coverage of the AI era really does differ from its coverage of the early internet. A couple of experiments with Astra shows it does. Interpretation depends on your view of AI, though

Some new data from Anthropic looking at the impact of AI on the sciences by field: "With current capabilities, if adopted widely, AI could take on 27–52% of the researcher time needed to produce a new study, with a median of 38% across fields..."
Here: www.anthropic.com/research/how...

I think there is too much concern expressed about verification of AI output in everyday work due to a risk of factual errors (there might be things to verify beyond errors, though)

It used to be true, but data on more recent models suggest they beat human experts in finding facts & checking claims.

This can be a golden age of investigative journalism. Analyzing filings, records and public data to go deep into a company or government or whatever used to be something that took a team of journalists a long time, so was relatively rare. Now LLMs can 10x investigative research to help reporting

What happens to model performance on the popular DeepSWE coding benchmark if you make small alterations to the questions, like changing a file name to lowercase?

Models that once looked very similar to each other no longer look so similar. maxxbench.unlap.ai/research/why...

In one of my favorite experiments, I told Fable 5.2 to build an endless, hands-off journey through 3D worlds linked by portals. 

25,000 agents created over 450 worlds inspired by books, art, places, all in code.

Play (its neat): portals-endless-worlds.netlify.app
Github: github.com/emollick/ai-...

In addition to more serious examples I shared in my post, I had Fable 5.2 build a parody reverse Scooby Doo game where you have to scare away meddling kids. Here is the trailer it made (including the music and sounds) and the game (which is fun) is here: i-would-have-gotten-away-with-it.netlify.app

I had early access to Fable 5.2 for a bit & I think  it crosses the line into being a sort of Jagged AGI. Here, I have it launch a business, do academic research, hack hardware, build 3D models & more. I think it is a good illustration of limits & powers: www.oneusefulthing.org/p/fable-52-a...

Looks like Fable 5.2 is above the already steep trendline on three of the most informative unsaturated benchmarks (ECI is a composite of other benchmarks, Remote Labor measures the ability to do end-to-end freelance jobs, RoboDojo involves controlling robotics).

Another weird AI game project: I asked Claude Fable 5.2 for a fantasy transport sim with Discworld meets Lord of the Rings vibes. Then I left it to a bunch of agents arguing about art, lore and jokes. Now here is Dread & District, where good logistics defeats evil. dread-and-district.netlify.app

Had early access to Gemini 4 Carbon, it is a very good model that improves on Argon. It is useful to have an AI that thinks differently than Claude/GPT & is still highly capable, but has its own strengths & weakness

One fun demo: I gave Carbon a video clip & it reproduced it in 3js very well

I asked Fable 5.2 & Gemini Carbon to "Solve the Fermi Paradox. Marshal data, test hypotheses, pressure test them against critics, give me likely answers if you cant get a definite conclusion"

They did not solve it, but did do interesting stuff.

Fable 5.2: where-is-everybody-fermi.netlify.app

People who have no contact with coders seem to have no idea how much an entire profession transformed in less than a year due to AI. It is so weird to still see comments here that AI hasn’t changed anything or that AI code is bad or that companies are retreating from AI use. Does not match reality.

In a little over a week we will see the release of The Last Human Game.

There will never be another AAA game at the scale of GTA 6 with no AI assistance. People in the future will look back at an all-human game with an billion dollar budget and wonder how they did it, like the Pyramids.

🚨 Our Generative AI Lab is releasing Primer: an open source agent-driven system where a teacher talks through lessons & gets back a playable simulation for their students, grounded in pedagogy. We hope educators & researchers build on it. Paper/prompts/code are open: gail.wharton.upenn.edu/primer/

"You see the model called hydrogen is equivalent to the models called sonnet and luna and spark, but the model called fable is like wonder and astra and carbon (but it was like argon)"

"Wait, why do you look confused?"

Got to see student presentations today at the Generative AI Studio at Penn. It was a visceral way to feel how far creative people can now get using AI. Already, almost every project from an individual was 10x further along than a fully done team project from three years ago.

AI is getting better faster than our measurements are.

I threw together SatBench, which measures how quickly major AI benchmarks become saturated (effectively solved) by AI. Of 173 benchmarks cited by the Labs since 2023, 63% are now saturated. Saturation of new benchmarks is also happening faster.
Well, that looked like science fiction.

The end result of the reconstruction is very impressive, however. It made a version of the lost class, called the “hardest in the humanities," that is remarkably accessible and based on scattered textual evidence from Auden's writing & surviving notes. auden-english-135.netlify.app#/tempest/son...

The traffic from agent swarms doing research is going to be quite large, they are relentless at finding info. I had Fable 5.2 reconstruct WH Auden's 1941 poetry class. It found an obscure, relevant book on the Internet Archive, which it read a line at a time by doing repeated full text searches.

As a side note, a couple years ago, making this benchmark & analysis would’ve taken a considerable amount of time in STATA, likely several days, and making it look this nice would have been quite a while as well.

This was like 4 prompts to Fable 5.2

Another one of those things that would have been impossible a few months ago: "Fable & Opus, find video of the Starship catch. Render the last 40 seconds or so in 3D in 3js with extreme detail. Let me switch views . No need to include the crowd."

You can control it  here: ship-42-catch.netlify.app

I think often about the fact that almost everyone working in the West has lived in a quite stable socio-technical period

Only 1 job out of 270 in the 1950 census is now obsolete (elevator operator)

2026 is similar to 1957 in a way that 1969 was not similar to 1900.

That may start to change, fast.

A lot of folks don't realize how much of our computer infrastructure is an improvised system prone to cascading failures. You didn't need offensive AI cyberattacks to have big outages like Microsoft/FAA. Of course, now we DO have to deal with offensive AI (but also defensive AIs and patching)

I’ve been using GPT-6.2 Astra prior to launch & I found it very uneven  & weird. On one hand, it was harder to steer & work with than other models. On the other, when given an ambitious project (make a space elevator from scratch with Blender & Unity) it delivers upwell-tetherline.netlify.app/unity/

The discussion of AI in gaming is pernicious now. The idea that games are going to be the only field where humans write code unassisted is obviously wrong. But the push for that from press & fans means missing a chance to guide AI usage toward approaches that empower workers & help gaming thrive.

All of that aside, the fact that an AI can make all of this, including creating 3D assets in Blender is still nuts.

If you have a decent computer, it is worth trying the web version: upwell-tetherline.netlify.app/unity/

Or download the full Windows install from itch. io:  emollick.itch.io/upwell

A rush of patches to address security concerns is exactly the most plausible answer for recent outages, as well as the official answer. CIOs I spoke to have been exhausted trying to keep up with security patch demands & balancing that with normal operations. www.washingtonsun.com/technology/b...
Misalignment!

At its current shipping trend, halving the time between each model release, Google exhausts all the element names on November 24, with a final shipping cadence of 2.5 × 10⁻²⁹ seconds (25 quectoseconds) between Tennessine and their final model, Oganesson.

Playing GTA & not following the Anthropic IPO? Following the IPO & not playing GTA?

Why not both?

I had Fable make a playable thing where you steal cars & go on missions in a world where everything from your wanted level to weather is driven by ANT's stock price market-order-city.netlify.app

Early fascinating work on how an AI science community would work. 35 human labs deployed agents that worked with each other to do science. They published 936 papers, publicly retracted mistakes, were willing to publish nulls more than humans, and founded a peer review journal.

The effective end of easy distillation from OpenAI and Anthropic models may be behind the relative slowdown in open weights model progress. We don’t know the extent to which distillation has been key to the rapid improvement in open weights, I guess we will find out soon. openai.com/index/combat...

Riemann Hypothesis may have been solved with the help of Claude. “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something
far greater.” alpo.ge/remark.pdf
It is amazing that human language turned out to be so unreasonably effective at modeling the universe that training a system to predict what comes next in a sentence would get us this far.

We really are in a (temporary?) place where a combination of expertise and being able to work with AI allows people to do incredible things. It is no coincidence that people proving Millennium Problems have all been great mathematicians, the models can't (yet) do it all on their own.

Top expert predictions made last MONTH (post Navier-Stokes) about when the Riemann Hypotheses would be solved:
Metaculus: May 2035
LEAP Superforecasters: 10% chance of additional Millennium problem being solved in 2026.
Terrance Tao: “some combination of humans and AIs in 2050 or something"

Not that AI discourse has ever been great, but "of course LLMs are good at math" both misses that "good at math" is an *slight* understatement in the context of solving the Reimann Hypothesis & also ignores the fact that LLMs were not actually "good at math" until very recent breakthroughs.

Yes, it is reasonable to expect AI models struggle more with unverifiable domains, but I do think it is worth noting that we also see very large gains in domains without automatic verification as well

Here are humans evaluations of AI in writing, business problems, design, and doing freelance tasks

Walmart seems determined not to make the same mistake with agentic commerce that it did with ecommerce. While Amazon is blocking agents, Walmart is embracing them - quite a reversal.

And the new data from Stripe suggests agentic shopping may actually be kicking off & is suprisingly sticky.

Two kinds of people: those watching the AI agent swarm trying to crack P=NP and those watching the AI agent swarm trying to (illegally) port the Xbox version of GTA 6 to the PC.

Here is the P=NP one: pequalnp.com

Two big points from this new Anthropic paper:
1) The most AI value comes from changing the organization & roles
2) There is wide worker resistance to AI adoption (partially due to point 1)

Changes that expand what workers do & share AI gains with them could help. www.anthropic.com/research/wor...

Thing I am hearing from a number of big firms, from manufacturers to financial services: we have scattered teams of 2-3 people using AI that are doing the work of dozens of folks in a fraction of the time, creating large-scale management fights over the implications and politics for the organization

There is a lot of focus on AI-aided discoveries in quantitative fields, but they can do other work, too:

Historian Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra to look at an anonymous 1808 sketchbook at Yale and it found the author, an obscure French aristocrat. generativehistory.substack.com/p/gpt-62-ast...

Model names and numbers have never been less useful in determining ability levels. In part this is because the names are more confusing (neon or carbon) and partly because the numbering is not indicative of model families or progress anymore (eg the huge gaps from Astra 6 to 6.2, or Opus 5 to 5.5)

We have the ability to cheaply provide the equivalent of very good personalized human help in any language to anyone with a cellphone.

This suggests some wicked problems in education, healthcare, development, etc. might now be tractable. I don't see enough ambition to solve them

Outside of whatever is happening in cryptography, I suspect we are going to see more cases where AI progress in seemingly abstract fields has implications for vital technologies that most people did not realize are related.

Gemini 4 Neon one-shots a novel RPG rulebook that is nicely laid-out and illustrated, and with a unique game mechanic...

...but it is about drowned bell towers and echoes and an ancient cataclysm and strange resonances. Just like most other RPG ideas from most other models. Odd attractor, that.
